Research: rates, timing and the six markets

Where rates are headed, when to buy, and how each region is doing.

Mortgage rates

Where rates are

  • 30-year fixed: 7.18% on Nov 5 (Freddie Mac). Down three weeks in a row, from 7.32% on Oct 22.
  • 15-year fixed: 6.57%.
  • A year ago: 6.22%. Rates are about 1 point higher than last fall.
  • Credit gap: a 620 score paid 7.17% and a 700 paid 6.61% on the same 30-year loan (Curinos via Experian, Feb 2026).

Where forecasters see them going

  • Fannie Mae (Oct): 7.4% this quarter, averaging 7.5% through 2027. Raised from 6.7% last month.
  • MBA (Oct): about 7.3% this quarter, above 7% all of 2027, 7.0% by the end of 2028.
  • Older forecasts of 5.9% to 6.7% for 2027 are out of date.

What it means for us

  • Don't wait for rates. Neither forecaster sees real relief in 2027.
  • Refinance later if rates fall. Each 0.25 point is about $150 a month on a $900,000 loan.
  • Credit matters more than timing. Brandon's score sets the rate and the mortgage insurance. The Affordability tab shows how much.
  • Ask builders about buydowns. New construction is where sellers pay for a lower rate.

Best time to buy

What the studies say

  • Redfin: August is the best month to buy. More listings, and sellers start offering concessions.
  • Realtor.com: late September and early October in most big metros.
  • Zillow: homes listed in late May sell fastest and for a bit more. Spring costs the most.
  • Late fall: early November to mid-December is the best window in some metros (Redfin).

What the local numbers say

  • Central NJ is softening. Somerset: 31 days on market, 15.6% of listings cut. Monmouth: 25 days, 17.3% cut (Prodigy, Sept).
  • Pennsylvania suburbs stay fast. Montgomery and Bucks sold in about 7 days in July.
  • Nassau and Westchester stay tight. Few listings: 33 to 35 days in Nassau, 2.6 months of supply in Westchester.

Our read

  • Now through January is off-peak. Less competition and more motivated sellers, but fewer homes.
  • Pennsylvania: little room to negotiate any time of year.
  • Central and Northern NJ: the best shot at a price cut or seller credit this winter.
  • School year: to move by August, sign in winter and close in summer.

How this list was built

What is in the list

  • Source: Redfin active listings. School ratings, tax and features come from the Redfin listing page or, where Redfin's page wasn't read, the Movoto listing page (same GreatSchools ratings). Every home also has a Zillow lookup link.
  • Filters: $650,000 to $1,200,000, 3+ bedrooms, any build year, in the six regions.
  • Schools: the average GreatSchools rating of the public schools that serve the address must be 7 or better. One school can be lower. A listing with no schools shown is left out.
  • Year built: as Redfin lists it, any year. 2025 or later is tagged New build and may not be finished.

What is not in the list

  • No year built: listings that don't show one can't be checked and are left out.
  • Missing listings: Redfin's feed leaves some out under MLS rules, so a home may exist that isn't here.
  • Distances are straight-line miles from the map pin, not drive or train time.
  • Taxes and insurance come from the listing. Movoto has no insurance figure, so those homes use the region's typical Redfin rate, marked estimated. If a new build's tax bill covers only the land, we use the region's typical rate and mark it on the home.

What our savings buy

Brandon's score, step by step

How approval works

The steps

  • Pre-approval: the lender checks credit and income papers and writes a letter with your maximum loan. Sellers expect it with an offer.
  • Papers: two years of W-2s and tax returns, 30 days of pay stubs, two months of bank statements, photo ID.
  • Underwriting: starts once a contract is signed. They recheck everything and order the appraisal and title search.
  • Clear to close: one last check just before closing. Keep your finances frozen until the keys are in hand.

Income

  • Gross pay: they use income before taxes.
  • Salary: counts once they verify the job, often with a call to the employer near closing.
  • Bonus or commission: usually needs two years of history and is averaged.
  • Who counts: only people on the loan. Wife alone is her $165,000. Both is $405,000, with both credit reports.
  • New job or a gap: expect questions and a letter.

Debt-to-income (DTI)

  • The math: the new house payment plus your other monthly debts, divided by gross monthly income.
  • New house payment: principal, interest, tax, insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA.
  • Other debts: car loans, student loans, minimum card payments. Rent and utilities don't count.
  • The limit: this page uses 45% conventional and 50% FHA. You can change both.
  • Why it matters: DTI sets the top price as much as income does. Paying off a car loan helps.

Credit

  • The score they use: the middle of the three bureau scores, for each borrower.
  • Minimums: conventional usually 620. FHA 580 for 3.5% down. A lender can set a higher bar.
  • Two borrowers: pricing and mortgage insurance use the lower score (Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-5.1-02). Approval can use the average. Fannie's Desktop Underwriter has done this; ask each lender.
  • So: her 750 doesn't lift his 600. At best the average gets the loan approved. The 600 still sets the rate.
  • What hurts it: late payments, collections, card balances over about 30% of the limit.

Down payment and cash

  • 20% down: no private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan.
  • Closing costs: separate cash, set by the percent in the box above.
  • Reserves: lenders may want a few months of payments left in savings. Bigger loans often want more.
  • Appraisal: the house has to appraise at the price. If it comes in low, you cover the gap.

Your bank statements

  • How far back: usually the last two months, every page, for each account that funds the purchase.
  • Investment and retirement accounts: the latest statement, often quarterly.
  • Seasoned money: funds sitting in an account for 60 days need no explanation.
  • New money: any deposit that isn't a paycheck gets a paper trail request. Big ones, about half a month's income or more, always do. Some lenders ask about much smaller ones.
  • If closing slips: they ask for the newest statement again.

In your bank account: do

  • Pay in: paychecks, into the same account, every time.
  • Move money between your own accounts only with statements from both ends.
  • Gifts: a signed gift letter from the giver, plus proof of the transfer.
  • Selling stock: keep the sale confirmation and the deposit record.
  • Keep all pages of every statement, even the blank ones.

In your bank account: avoid

  • Cash deposits. They can't be traced.
  • Overdrafts and bounced payments. They look like cash trouble.
  • Big Venmo, Zelle or Cash App transfers from friends or family without a gift letter.
  • Crypto buys and gambling charges. Both get questioned.
  • New loan or payment plan charges, including buy-now-pay-later.
  • Drawing the down payment down to near zero. Leave a cushion for reserves.

What each loan type asks

  • Conventional: 620 at most lenders, 3% to 5% down at the low end, mortgage insurance until 20% equity.
  • FHA: 580 for 3.5% down. Easier on score, but insurance lasts the life of the loan with under 10% down. County loan limits apply.
  • Jumbo: a loan above the conforming limit. This page assumes a 700 score and 20% down. Expect bigger reserves.

What lenders look for

  • Income: steady, documented, and enough to stay under the DTI limit.
  • Credit: a middle score that clears the minimum and a clean recent record.
  • Cash: down payment, closing costs and reserves, all traceable.
  • The house: it appraises at the price and meets the loan's condition rules.
  • Nothing new: a new debt or job change is the usual reason a deal stalls.

Where to compare rates

  • No single best lender. The same borrower gets different rates and fees at different lenders.
  • Credit unions: often low fees. PenFed or Navy Federal if you're eligible, or a local PA or NJ credit union.
  • Your own bank: ask about a discount for the accounts you already have.
  • Online lenders: Rocket Mortgage, Better, loanDepot. Quick quotes.
  • Mortgage brokers: one application, quotes from many lenders. Ask what they charge.
  • To check a quote: Freddie Mac's weekly average, Bankrate, NerdWallet, the CFPB rate tool.
  • Compare: get 3 to 5 written Loan Estimates the same day, same points, same rate lock. Mortgage credit checks within a few weeks of each other count as one.
  • State programs: NJHMFA in New Jersey and PHFA in Pennsylvania help some buyers. Ask about income limits.
  • Examples only, not endorsements.

Get ready now

  • Pull all three credit reports free at annualcreditreport.com. Dispute errors first; fixes take weeks.
  • Pay cards down below about 30% of each limit. Lower is better. It moves the score fastest, and a lender can rescore quickly once balances update.
  • Gather the papers: two years of W-2s and returns, recent pay stubs, two months of statements.
  • Park the down payment in one account for at least two months.
  • Add up real monthly debts, including the planned car payment.
  • Pick a path: wife alone, or both at the 600. See what a higher score would change.

Stop until closing

  • Opening cards or loans, including store cards and furniture financing.
  • Buying the car first. A new car loan raises DTI and lowers the top price.
  • Closing old cards. It can lower the score.
  • Changing jobs or pay without telling the lender.
  • Moving big money around.
  • Missing a payment, even by a few days.
  • Co-signing for anyone.

How the numbers work

The four approaches

  • Wife alone: $165,000 income, 750 score. Best rate, lowest ceiling.
  • Both, lowest score: $405,000 income, 600 score. Conventional needs 620, so this is FHA.
  • Both, scores averaged: approved on the average if the lender allows it, priced at the 600. Some lenders use the lower score instead.
  • Both, after the score goal: the same joint loan once Brandon hits the goal score in the box.

How the rate is built

  • Base: the Freddie Mac average (7.18%) is for a strong borrower with 20% down. It's the 740+ line here. You can change it.
  • Score adders: conventional rates rise about 0.1 to 0.2 points per 20 points of score below 740, and faster below 680. FHA starts 0.25 lower and moves less.
  • Mortgage insurance: conventional under 20% down costs 0.25% to 2.6% of the loan a year, by score. FHA is 1.75% up front plus 0.50% to 0.75% a year, for the life of the loan when down is under 10%.
  • Jumbo: above the conforming limit this page needs a 700 score and 20% down, and adds 0.15 to the rate.
  • Estimates, not quotes.

Loan limits

  • Conforming, 2026: $832,750 baseline, $1,249,125 in high-cost counties (NYC-area NJ and NY).
  • FHA: the high-cost NJ and NY counties go to $1,249,125. PA and South Jersey sit near $568,000 to $630,000 (Bucks $630,200), too low for this price range.
  • Check the county on HUD's and FHFA's lookup tools.

Ask every lender

  • Score rule: average or lowest, and their minimum.
  • Debts: the $700 default covers a planned car payment. Use the real total.
  • Income: how they count bonus or variable pay.
  • Rates move daily. Get a written estimate for each path.
